lead: The DC bus sets the square-wave inverter output, so the fundamental peak is fixed at 4V<sub>dc</sub>/π, that is 1.273V<sub>dc</sub>. To change the output voltage without changing V<sub>dc</sub>, cut zero-voltage notches into each half cycle. Single-pulse modulation gives one pulse per half cycle; with d as half the pulse width, the pulse is 2d wide and the zero-voltage notches, each π−2d wide, sit on either side of every zero crossing. Multiple-pulse modulation gives p equal pulses per half cycle, each of width 2d. Both keep the switches hard on or hard off, so efficiency stays high. They appear in older variable-voltage drives, induction heating, UPS units and cheap fan or pump inverters, before sinusoidal PWM took over.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for the square wave and its 4Vdc/π fundamental.

sections.h3: The fixed square wave and the notch

blocks.text: A full-bridge inverter switches the load between +V<sub>dc</sub> and −V<sub>dc</sub>. With no control, the output is a square wave. Its fundamental peak is fixed at 4V<sub>dc</sub>/π, which is 1.273V<sub>dc</sub>. If V<sub>dc</sub> comes from a battery or a rectifier that you do not want to vary, you cannot change the AC voltage by changing the bus.

The fix is to insert zero-voltage intervals, called notches, into each half cycle. Keep the switches either fully on or fully off. In the positive half cycle, the output is +V<sub>dc</sub> for a pulse of width 2d centred at 90°, and zero for the rest. The negative half cycle mirrors it. The result is a quasi-square wave: a square wave with a bite taken out. One pulse per half cycle is single-pulse modulation, also called notch modulation. Several equal pulses per half cycle give multiple-pulse modulation, also called uniform PWM. The DC bus stays fixed; the pulse width sets the output voltage.
Let d be half the pulse width, measured in radians. The pulse width is 2d. The fundamental peak is given by the formula below. If your d is in degrees, use sin(d×π/180) inside the sine.

blocks.where: V<sub>1p</sub> is the fundamental peak voltage in V; V<sub>dc</sub> is the DC bus voltage in V; d is half the pulse width in radians inside the sine.

blocks.text: The rms output over a half cycle is set by the total on-time. With d in radians, use the next formula. With d in degrees, the same result is V<sub>dc</sub>√(d/90). At d = 90°, the pulse fills the half cycle, so V<sub>1p</sub> = 4V<sub>dc</sub>/π and V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>dc</sub>. At d = 0, the output is zero.

blocks.where: V<sub>rms</sub> is the rms output voltage in V; V<sub>dc</sub> is the DC bus voltage in V; d is half the pulse width in radians.

blocks.text: The control is not linear. Near d = 90°, sin d changes slowly, so a large change in d gives a small change in fundamental. Near d = 0, sin d ≈ d, so the fundamental is almost proportional to d. The nth harmonic amplitude for odd n is (4V<sub>dc</sub>/(nπ)) sin(n d). The 3rd harmonic is strong for most d, which is why single-pulse output needs a filter.

Split each half cycle into p equal pulses, each of width 2d and equally spaced. The total on-time in a half cycle is 2pd radians. The rms output is given by the formula below. If each pulse is w degrees wide, the on fraction is p w /180, so V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>dc</sub>√(p w/180). The formula uses p pulses per half cycle; a full cycle has 2p pulses.

blocks.where: V<sub>rms</sub> is the rms output voltage in V; V<sub>dc</sub> is the DC bus voltage in V; p is the number of equal pulses per half cycle; d is half of one pulse width in radians.

blocks.text: The lowest strong harmonic moves up to about order 2p−1. For p = 2, the first strong group is near the 3rd; for p = 4, near the 7th; for p = 6, near the 11th. Higher p means the filter can be smaller, because the ripple is at a higher frequency. The price is switching loss. Each pulse has two edges, so p pulses per half cycle give 2p pulses and 4p switching transitions per cycle. More transitions mean more switching loss in the devices and more gate-drive power.

Choose p from the allowed harmonic spectrum and the switching-loss budget. Audio noise also matters: a low-order harmonic can make a motor or inductor sing. For the same total on-time, the rms stays the same when p changes, but the harmonic positions change. That is the trade-off: p buys harmonic quality with switching loss.

figure.caption: The upper curve is the fundamental peak in per unit of V<sub>dc</sub>; the lower curve is the rms output, both against half-pulse width d from 0° to 90°. At d = 30° the curves read about 0.64 and 0.58 per unit, the values used in the worked example.

spec.aria: Two curves against pulse half-width d: the fundamental follows a sine and peaks at 1.27 times Vdc at d = 90 degrees, while the rms rises as the square root of the on-time and reaches Vdc at d = 90 degrees.

examples.question: A full-bridge inverter has V<sub>dc</sub> = 200 V. (a) It uses single-pulse modulation with d = 30°. Find the fundamental peak and the rms output. (b) It is changed to 4 equal pulses per half cycle, each 10° wide. Find the new rms output and the approximate order of the first strong harmonic.
steps: For (a), convert d: 30° = π/6 rad = 0.5236 rad.
For (b), total on-time per half cycle = 4×10° = 40°.
examples.answer: The single-pulse case gives a fundamental peak of 127.3 V and rms of 115.5 V; with four pulses the rms is 94.3 V and the first strong harmonic is near the 7th order.
examples.check:
import math
Vdc = 200
d_deg = 30
d = math.radians(d_deg)
V1 = 4 * Vdc / math.pi * math.sin(d)
Vrms_a = Vdc * math.sqrt(2 * d / math.pi)
p = 4
w = 10
on_deg = p * w
Vrms_b = Vdc * math.sqrt(on_deg / 180)
h = 2 * p - 1
print(round(V1, 1))
print(round(Vrms_a, 1))
print(round(Vrms_b, 1))
print(h)

traps: Putting degrees into sin without converting: sin 30 is not 0.5 on a calculator set to radians. Convert d to radians or use sin(d×π/180).
Assuming the fundamental falls linearly with pulse width: it follows sin d, so halving d near 90° does not halve the fundamental.
Calling p the pulses per cycle: the formulas use p pulses per half cycle, so a full cycle has 2p pulses and 4p switching transitions, not p pulses and 2p transitions.
Confusing rms with fundamental peak: rms is set by total on-time, not by pulse position; the fundamental also depends on where the pulses sit.
Forgetting the first strong harmonic order: for multiple-pulse modulation it is about 2p−1, not 2p+1; single-pulse modulation still has a strong 3rd harmonic.

quiz.q: What is single-pulse modulation in a voltage-source inverter?
quiz.a: Single-pulse modulation gives one pulse of width 2d per half cycle, and the zero-voltage notches (each of width π−2d) sit on either side of each zero crossing. The DC bus stays fixed and d controls the fundamental.

quiz.q: Why does the fundamental peak fall as sin d and not linearly with d?
quiz.a: The pulse is a window of the square wave. Its overlap with the fundamental sine is proportional to sin d. Near d = 90° the sine flattens, so large width changes give small fundamental changes.

quiz.q: A full bridge has V<sub>dc</sub> = 300 V and uses single-pulse modulation with d = 45°. Find the fundamental peak and the rms output.
A full bridge has V<sub>dc</sub> = 250 V and uses 3 equal pulses per half cycle, each 15° wide. Find the rms output and the first strong harmonic order.
quiz.a: Total on-time per half cycle = 3×15° = 45°. On fraction = 45/180 = 0.25. V<sub>rms</sub> = 250×√0.25 = 125 V. First strong harmonic order ≈ 2×3−1 = 5.

quiz.q: Increasing p from 2 to 6 at the same total on-time: what happens to rms, first strong harmonic, and switching loss?
quiz.a: The rms stays the same because total on-time is the same. The first strong harmonic moves from about the 3rd to about the 11th. Switching loss increases because there are more pulse edges per cycle.

quiz.q: Why does multiple-pulse modulation push the first strong harmonic to about order 2p−1?
quiz.a: Equal pulses and equal spacing cancel lower-order components by symmetry. The first significant group appears around the pulse count, roughly 2p−1.

quiz.q: Give the other common names for single-pulse and multiple-pulse modulation.
quiz.a: Single-pulse modulation is also called notch modulation or quasi-square-wave modulation. Multiple-pulse modulation is also called uniform PWM.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern drives usually replace these fixed-angle methods with sinusoidal PWM (Chapter 4.4) or space vector modulation (Chapter 4.5), because a high switching frequency pushes harmonics above the audible and filter range. Selective harmonic elimination (Chapter 4.6) keeps the low switching count but solves for notch angles. Wide-bandgap SiC and GaN devices make high-frequency PWM cheaper in loss, which is why multiple-pulse uniform PWM is mostly a teaching step today. Search 'selective harmonic elimination inverter', 'programmed PWM' and 'quasi-square wave inverter'.
